grammar.title: Frase
grammar.rule: uma bolsa azul → duas bolsas azuis; um livro branco → dois livros brancos.
grammar.note_en:
Plural means more than one. This chapter changes the number of things named while keeping a singular subject—one person or thing—with each finite verb. Ana vê duas bolsas azuis means “Ana sees two blue bags”; Bia mostra os dois livros brancos means “Bia shows the two white books.” Vê and mostra still describe one person doing the seeing or showing. The nouns after them name several objects. We have not introduced plural verb forms: do not change these verbs merely because the objects are plural.

A noun names a thing or person. An article is a word such as o/a or um/uma accompanying it. An adjective describes it, such as azul or diferente. These words agree: their forms match the noun’s number and, where the word distinguishes it, its grammatical gender. Gender is the noun’s masculine or feminine class, not a claim about the object’s sex. Compare uma bolsa azul (“a blue bag”) with duas bolsas azuis (“two blue bags”), and um livro branco (“a white book”) with dois livros brancos (“two white books”). One bag becomes several bolsas; one book several livros. The definite articles become os/as: os livros means “the books,” as bolsas “the bags.” Dois accompanies masculine nouns, duas feminine ones. Três, quatro and cinco mean “three,” “four” and “five”; their forms do not change between the masculine and feminine nouns here.

Many plurals here add s: livro → livros (“book → books”), chave → chaves (“key → keys”), nome → nomes (“name → names”), cadeira → cadeiras (“chair → chairs”), caderno → cadernos (“notebook → notebooks”). Do not turn that common pattern into an exceptionless rule. Azul → azuis means “blue” for one versus several things, and igual → iguais means “same/alike” for one versus several. Papel → papéis means “sheet of paper → sheets of paper”; note both the changed ending and written accent. The accent remains part of standard spelling even when answer checking tolerates its omission. Diferente → diferentes means “different” for one versus several and uses the same form for masculine and feminine nouns of that number. In two blue bags, both bags can look alike while their books and owners differ. Igual does not claim the objects are literally the same physical bag.

Contractions agree with the following plural noun: em + os becomes nos, de + os becomes dos, and de + as becomes das. O nome nos livros é diferente means “The name in the books is different”; os nomes dos donos means “the owners’ names”; uma das duas bolsas means “one of the two bags.” The singular phrase remains no livro (“in the book”), do dono (“of the male owner”), da bolsa (“of the bag”); das duas bolsas means “of the two bags,” and dos donos “of the male owners.” The table labels de / em + o / a and de / em + os / as contrast singular and plural article combinations, not additional story forms. In uma das duas bolsas, uma picks one bag from a plural group. In três livros, dois livros brancos e um livro preto (“three books, two white books and one black book”), the smaller groups account for the total. These are object groups, not new plural verb patterns.

Troca means “exchanges”: Ana troca a bolsa means “Ana exchanges the bag.” The narrated handover explains which bag she takes and which she leaves. Volta means “returns/comes back”; O livro volta means “The book comes back.” Chega means “arrives”; chega perto de Paulo means “comes up near Paulo.” Leva means “takes/carries away,” whereas deixa in these object scenes means “leaves/puts down”: Paulo leva sua bolsa means “Paulo takes his bag with him”; Paulo deixa a caixa means “Paulo puts down the box.” Lê means “reads”; Rosa lê os nomes means “Rosa reads the names.” These are the actual third-person singular present forms used here, not a full conjugation. The old notebook’s number 2019, gathering photograph, 20:00 and dark window establish an earlier night; the narration still reports present seeing and reading. No past tense is required. Novo/velho mean “new/old” for the masculine notebooks; noite means “night.” Rosa’s new list includes Ana, who is absent from the old photograph. The question Uma noite no café? (“A night at the café?”), answered by Rosa and the shown name, proposes a new gathering; the chapter does not claim it has already taken place.

The first table compares one thing with two, including uma bolsa igual (“one matching bag”) and duas bolsas iguais (“two matching bags”), um papel (“one sheet of paper”) and dois papéis (“two sheets of paper”). The adjective and paper-form contrasts are now complete phrases under matching numeral headings.
